# Xtreme Vibing: values, principles, and practices

The values, principles, and practices of Xtreme Vibing. The last table shows where each XP practice went.

## Values

| Value | What we mean |
| --- | --- |
| Build for users | Value is the experience of the person using the software. Understanding users and creating value for them is the job of everyone on the team. Work that is not for their good is refused. |
| Be empirical | We decide from evidence of real use, not from what we expect. A decision about what the user experiences is void without a recent session with users or a packet from real use. Prototypes are run and compared, not argued. Standards are earned by misses. Budgets are corrected by what the work actually spent. The process itself is a hypothesis: we start with the best we know and refine it as we work. Everyone on the team is learning, by doing. |
| Invest in trust | The team must trust each other and the system they use to build the system. The people who fund the software must trust the team with the product. Trust is earned, and it is necessary for speed. |

Discipline is not a value. It is what XV is: discipline at speed. Some of it is enforced by agents and the pipeline. The rest is owned by the people.

Two things exist before the work starts and are not values. The mission says why we are here. The vision says what the solution is becoming. The team is responsible for knowing both, and uses them to refuse work. The business's goals enter there and stop there. The business does not decide details.

Shareholder return was set by the people who funded the software, before this team. It does not affect the ranking of work.

A stakeholder is not a user. A product owner is one user, at best, and is most likely a proxy. Sitting with either one is not sitting with the people who use the system.

## Principles

Principles are the bridge between the values and the practices, as they were in XP. They say how a person decides, whatever the practice. Every practice feeds one of the first two. Go and see says where the evidence comes from. Ship at will opens the gate. Own the result closes the loop.

| Principle | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Decide from evidence | Two or more people work through the same packet and decide. This is the pair programming of XV. They name which difference mattered or which cost is worth paying. The decision is written down short, with who took part, and binds later agents. This covers a usability prototype pick, a shape change that adds an abstraction, and an edit that changes what the system is for. The shape conversation's standing moments (before a burst and as it ends) can open it. Contact and Parallel prototypes feed it. The guardian identifies a shape change and produces the packet. The packet always includes access to the raw data. The form stays the team's. There is no approve button. A team of one runs the same stops: one person answers, and the record says one person decided. |
| Lead with conviction | One person who is accountable decides from experience, responsibility, and judgment. They are data-informed. The engineer making a change has the right and the duty to make it alone, unless the guardian, or they themselves, call for a second human. Typical cases: ranking the value queue, where evidence from use feeds the ranking and rarely settles the order, so the order is the ranking person's conviction (no separate recorded reasons; a ranking with no recent session or packet behind it is still void); a performance or narrow approach on the change being made, when the choice stays inside the current shape; an old test that changed, when the shape did not; a change to the shared operating picture that is not a shape or pitch change. This is collective ownership in XV. Anyone may change what a scenario requires. No one personally owns a file or subsystem. Agents build. The person who set the work going accepts it and ships it to production. Any teammate may do that in their place. The decision is not written down unless it will make a future job easier. If the guardian flags a shape change, it escalates to Decide from evidence. Generating axes for Parallel prototypes does not require a second human. |
| Go and see | Lean's genchi genbutsu: go to the real place and look at the real thing before you decide. In software the real place is where the system is used. It is not the code, and it is not the factory. A decision about what the user experiences is void without a recent session with users or a packet from real use. That is the ranking, a prototype pick where the axis was the interaction, an edit to the pitch, and a shape change justified by what the user needs. The packet says what the raw data means, and carries the raw data with it: the diff, the telemetry, the session recordings. A person reads the meaning first, and may go into the raw, with an agent's help if they like. A report that cannot be checked against the real thing does not count. A packet alone may rank a small slice. It may not harden a shape or rewrite the pitch. A meeting is not contact. |
| Ship at will | The gate is released to the person. The harness sets the conditions: red before green, the test wall, the three agents, and a build that returns in minutes. When they are met, the person who set the work going, the originator, merges and picks the moment. Any teammate may do it in their place. Nobody else approves. A required approval is the right gate for strangers, which is why open source needs it. On a team it becomes the process, and collaboration moves to the fence. |
| Own the result | A person is responsible for the consequences of every change, including one made entirely by agents. This is why the harness may stop and may not decide. The watch is the agent that stops. When it sees a shape change, a pitch contradiction, a spent budget, changed tests, or a changed picture, it stops and puts the decision in front of a person, and that person answers. When production raises its hand, the person who set the work going answers first. A check that cannot run is not a pass; it stops for a person. Nobody hands a result to the machine. |

## Practices

### Of the team

| Practice | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| The shared operating picture | The team's current understanding, written down: the users, what the system is right now, and ideas for how it can better represent the vision. It does not repeat what the code says. It is enough for a new person, or an agent, to understand the context: the shape, the names, the decisions that bind, who the users are, what is in motion. Agents pull it, or parts of it, when needed. It is not loaded by default. Yesterday's change is part of today's picture, and that change rides in the packet, accepted by the person who set the work going. A change to the shape or the pitch still takes two people. The name comes from the common operating picture of military and emergency operations. |
| The shape | The structure of the system as the team can observe it: design concerns such as coupling, and runtime concerns such as response time budgets. A change to the shape is decided by people in conversation, not with an approve button. A cleanup that adds an abstraction is a shape change, not a cleanup. Work tends to come in bursts, and the shape is rethought before a burst and as it ends. |
| The value queue | One person ranks the work by customer value, so the ranking is a decision and the product stays one product. Any teammate may take the next task. Responsibility for ranking work does not make customer value that person's job alone. A conflict between the user and the people paying gets escalated. |
| The pitch | A short page in the repo: what the system does, why, and for whom. An agent may not invent a second purpose. A change to it lands when a second person agrees. |
| Contact | Sit with the people who use the software, or with data about how they actually use it. The listener gathers that data into the packet; nobody holds the corpus. A meeting with a stakeholder is not contact with a user. |
| Parallel prototypes | For a change where the scenario does not settle the design, and a wrong design would be felt in use. Have agents build three running versions that differ on one named axis. At least two people choose between them by naming which difference mattered. One is chosen, or none. When the evaluated set points at a combination, or at a new direction, run another round. Involve real users whenever possible. A prototype may run in production for a few real users when that is the only way to learn. It is still discarded at the pick. |
| Attention | A person who is too tired or spread too thin does not make the call today. A teammate who is not fit to decide today is told so. Agents may run while a person is away. Decisions do not pile up. The pace stays human even while going fast. When the chief engineer is away, one designated person holds the value queue and the pitch; the duty does not become consensus. Decide from evidence requires a synchronous conversation, so the team keeps overlap in working hours. |

### Of the machine

The machine enforces these. The machine is the harness: the agents, the test suite, and the pipeline. The watch runs the pipeline. The agents, and how they work with people, are drawn in [the agents](/agents/).

| Practice | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| The test wall | A scenario made executable by the scenario agent, which is never the maker, and shown to fail before the fix. The existing suite is the wall. The maker may move an old test only when the scenario forces it, and records why. The scenario agent may mark tests that only prove this slice; the cleaner removes those after green with a record, no further person decision. The guardian lists every changed test, and any recommendation that a new test should stay or leave the wall, in the packet for the change. The person who set the work going accepts them, and decides whether to talk it through or ship. A shape change always goes to two people. |
| The budget | A budget on the task, forecast by the forecaster with the engineer who takes it, including an expectation of shape change and its breadth (none, narrow, or wide). When it is spent, the work stops, green or not, and a person decides whether the task was the wrong one. The budget is a ceiling, not a test. In [one estimation guide](https://github.com/seanpk/xv-agents/blob/v0.3.0/.xv/estimation.md) from use, forecasts missed by two to eight times when a person sent the work back. Learnings from estimate versus actual become team-wide; the forecaster updates an estimation guide from what the run spent. An individual may increase the budget and continue under Lead with conviction, up to a team-agreed limit; beyond that, or if the shape change is wider than expected, Decide from evidence. |
| The three agents | Three contexts on one change. The maker makes it work behind the test wall; it may move an old test only when the scenario forces it, with a record. The cleaner makes it right against the standards file it keeps, earned by repeated misses; it commits the fix, keeps old-test changes small, rejects a real test turned fake, and removes tests marked slice-only after green. Structure and behavior do not ride in one pass. The guardian, with an adversarial brief, checks for a shape change, a pitch contradiction, a changed test, a recommendation on which new tests join or leave the wall, and a changed picture, draws the boundary diagram, and produces the one packet for the change. Shape or pitch: the change stops for Decide from evidence. Tests or picture alone: the packet goes to the person who set the work going. Security and usability agents are guardian-kind. A prototype is a maker brief, in a context that never builds the pick. None of them merges. More of each may run. The contexts stay separate. |
| The watch | The agent that runs the pipeline. It knows the state of every slice, calls each agent in turn with a brief and a fresh context, keeps the log visible to anyone who needs it, and wakes a person on a standing order: the stops in the loop. A stop waits; the packet does not. It records who took part. It never decides: no merge, no ranking, no shape, and it never edits its own standing orders. From the bridge of a ship: it keeps the deck while the captain sleeps, and may wake the captain but may not change course. |
| The fast build | The merge waits on the pre-merge suite (the commit stage) that returns in minutes. A skipped suite is a failed build. Slow checks run post-merge; their failure reverts the main line and raises a new defect. Ten minutes is the inherited proxy, not a law. A slow suite is a defect in the suite. |
| Ship | An increment that cannot be used by a user is not done. The person who set the work going merges when the suite is green and the three agents have found no break that requires a person. Any teammate may do that in their place. No second person approves the merge. When production raises its hand, the person who set the work going answers first, and the listener brings what production says back as the packet. |

## The original twelve practices

| XP practice | What it was for | XV practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning game | Rank the next work by customer value, with the people who will do it | The value queue |
| Small releases | Put a thin slice in front of real use, often | Ship |
| Metaphor | One shared story of what the system is | The pitch |
| Simple design | The simplest thing that could work, for the need known today | The shape |
| Testing | Feedback from the system, with the dial turned up to test-first | The test wall |
| Refactoring | Keep the design fit to change, apart from new behavior | The three agents |
| Pair programming | A second mind on the work, all the time | Decide from evidence |
| Collective ownership | Anyone may change any part | Lead with conviction |
| Continuous integration | Integrate many times a day, so the trunk is the system | The fast build |
| Sustainable pace | The team can do this again tomorrow | Attention |
| On-site customer | A real user with the team, accepting the work | Contact |
| Coding standards | One team can read one another's work | The three agents |

Slack, from the 2004 edition, is The budget. Parallel prototypes are ours. They have no single parent in the twelve. Pair programming and collective ownership went to principles, not practices: the second mind and the right to change any part are now rules about how a person decides.
